existing_claim: Applies to every condo association of three or more habitable stories.
new_claim: By October 1, 2025, all condominium and cooperative associations are required to create an online account with the Division of Condominiums, Timeshares and Mobile Homes ... [and] associations are now required to complete a Structural Integrity Reserve Study by December 31, 2025.

existing_claim: Pairs with a separate 25-year milestone structural inspection requirement; the two studies are typically run by different firms and joined manually.
new_claim: The milestone inspection is triggered at 30 years of age and every 10 years thereafter, or at 25 years and every 10 years thereafter only if the local enforcement agency has determined that local circumstances require the initial milestone inspection at 25 years instead of 30 years.

existing_claim: CA, NJ, and VA legislation is in motion following Florida's lead.
new_claim: California already had a reserve study statute (Civil Code § 5550 within the Davis-Stirling Act) requiring triennial visual inspection and a reserve funding plan; SB 900 (Stats. 2024, Ch. 288, Sec. 2) effective January 1, 2025 amends the existing statute rather than introducing a new reserve study regime in CA's response to Florida.

existing_claim: Florida (SIRS / HB 913 & SB 4-D) — the Structural Integrity Reserve Study (SIRS) strictly focuses on eight critical building elements; associations must complete their SIRS by December 31, 2025; Florida law now requires associations to fully fund these structural reserves.
new_claim: The Florida Senate's official bill page for CS/CS/HB 913 (2025), Chapter 2025-175, characterizes the law's substantive content as community-association-manager licensure controls (post-revocation employment/ownership bans) and DBPR online-account requirements; the public-facing summary contains no SIRS, structural-element, or reserve-funding language.

existing_claim: Florida HB 913 (SIRS): Associations must complete a Structural Integrity Reserve Study (SIRS) by December 31, 2025. This mandates fully funded reserves for 8 critical elements (roofs, load-bearing structures, fire protection, plumbing, electrical, waterproofing/painting, windows/doors).
new_claim: The Florida Senate bill page for CS/CS/HB 913 (2025) summarizes HB 913 as a CAM-licensure / DBPR-online-account statute (post-revocation prohibitions, mandatory online accounts, firm-to-licensee identification) with no mention of SIRS, structural elements, fully-funded reserves, or a 2025 reserve-study deadline.

existing_claim: Florida's Structural Integrity Reserve Study (SIRS) (SB 4-D / HB 913) directly addresses deferred maintenance — mandates a SIRS by December 31, 2025, focuses on eight critical life-safety elements, and eliminates the historic ability for owners to vote to waive or partially fund those reserves.
new_claim: The Florida Senate's primary-source page for CS/CS/HB 913 (2025), Chapter 2025-175, describes HB 913 as a community-association-manager licensure and DBPR online-account bill, not as a structural-integrity reserve mandate — leaving open whether HB 913 truly contains the SIRS provisions attributed to it, or whether those provisions sit primarily in SB 4-D (2022) and only the manager-licensure layer sits in HB 913 (2025).

existing_claim: Florida CS/CS/HB 913 (2025), titled 'Condominium and Cooperative Associations' and codified as Chapter 2025-175, is a state law... [the] Senate's public bill page summarizes the law as a community-association-manager (CAM) licensure and Department of Business and Professional Regulation (DBPR) online-account regime, with post-revocation prohibitions on ownership and employment in CAM firms.
new_claim: Florida SB-4D / SIRS (HB 913, 2025) is forcing every 3+ story condo into mandatory reserve studies with no waivers — i.e., the source frames HB 913 (2025) as the bill establishing/extending the Structural Integrity Reserve Study regime, not (or not only) the CAM licensure regime described on the existing wiki page.

existing_claim: The Maintenance Matters series is produced in collaboration with Polygon and Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation [[sources/pdf-bc-housing-2020-maintenance-matters-06]].
new_claim: MM-02 (Maintaining Your Roof) is produced by BC Housing in collaboration with Polygon and the Condominium Home Owners' Association (CHOA), not CMHC — showing that collaborators on the Maintenance Matters series vary by bulletin rather than being a series-wide property.

existing_claim: Published by BC Housing in collaboration with Polygon and Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; content prepared by a consortium of building envelope experts [[sources/pdf-bc-housing-2020-maintenance-matters-06]].
new_claim: MM-02 lists Polygon and the Condominium Home Owners' Association (CHOA) — not CMHC — as collaborators alongside BC Housing, indicating the existing series-level claim overgeneralizes from a single bulletin's masthead.

existing_claim: The dataset is distributed as a 56 KiB XLSX in the NRC Research Data collection (DOI 10.4224/40003877), making it directly ingestible as a structured Bayesian-prior source without further extraction work [[sources/web-2026-05-10-f34]].
new_claim: Nearly half of the EPDs reviewed entirely ignore mentioning the RSL values; among those that include RSL, many rely on a default 75-year building lifespan without evidence or justification; and remaining EPDs present widely differing values for identical products — collectively meaning the dataset is structurally easy to load but the underlying values inherit EPD quality issues that require provenance-aware handling rather than direct use as point priors [[sources/web-2026-05-11-852]].

existing_claim: The NRC dataset is published as a tabular XLSX file, making it directly ingestible as a structured prior source for component-level survival models without further extraction work [[sources/web-2026-05-10-f34]].
new_claim: RSL is a key source of uncertainty in LCAs; the NRC dataset's EPD-derived RSL values exhibit missing entries (~half of EPDs lack RSL), unjustified 75-year-lifespan defaults, and wide per-product variance, meaning the values themselves are noisy priors even though the file format is easy to load [[sources/web-2026-05-11-852]].

existing_claim: A reserve fund is used to pay for the major repairs and replacement of common property (such as replacing the roof or painting the outside of the building), and reserve-fund monies may only pay for major expenses — not emergencies or unexpected expenses, which must be covered by a separately established contingency fund [[sources/web-2017-07-26-1f3]].
new_claim: Substantial changes to the common elements and assets — adding to, altering, improving or renovating the common elements — are considered common expenses and are paid out of the corporation's reserve fund (provided owners holding at least 60 percent of the common elements approve) [[sources/web-2018-03-31-c63]].

existing_claim: The regime requires full funding of the structural reserves; owner waivers and partial-funding votes are no longer permitted.
new_claim: Under CS/CS/HB 913 (2025), unit owners may vote to use a line of credit in lieu of fully funding reserves annually (with notice and disclosure requirements); members of a unit-owner-controlled association may approve a secured line of credit by majority vote to meet the SIRS-recommended reserve funding schedule; a board may pause reserve contributions without member approval if a local building official determines the building is uninhabitable due to a natural emergency; and members may vote to waive the maintenance of reserves recommended by the most recent SIRS if the association votes to terminate the condominium.

existing_claim: Serves more than 20,000 homeowners associations and 2 million homes (per May 2, 2023 SmartProperty integration announcement).
new_claim: Serves more than 4 million units across about 35,000 associations and nearly 800 management companies (per December 14, 2023 Hg investment announcement).

existing_claim: The amendments require more frequent reserve-fund studies to help corporations plan for future capital repairs.
new_claim: Nova Scotia's mandatory reserve-fund-study cadence is every 10 years, with a site inspection every 10 years and a minimum 30-year planning horizon — placing NS as the longest base reserve-fund-study cycle in the Canadian provincial comparator set.

existing_claim: NB's reserve-fund-study regime sets a 10-year primary cadence with 3-year updates and a 30-year forward horizon — broadly comparable to NL Condominium Regulations NLR 80/11's 30-year minimum recommended funding plan but with a longer base cycle than BC SPA's 5-year cycle or CA Davis-Stirling § 5550's triennial visual inspection.
new_claim: The Atlantic provinces and the North operate under 'more discretionary frameworks' in contrast to the highly prescriptive regimes in Ontario, British Columbia, and Quebec.

existing_claim: The Bill 16 explanatory notes do not surface a statutory cadence, qualified-preparer professional set, or prescribed-contents structure analogous to BC SPA's 5-year cycle, six-profession qualified-provider restriction, or Strata Property Regulation 6.2 physical-inventory-and-evaluation requirement, leaving operational discretion to the Civil Code article-level text and subordinate Quebec regulations.
new_claim: Quebec's contingency-fund-study cadence is every 5 years and the legislation emphasizes a 25-year planning horizon, with annual contributions required to be based on realistic professional assessments of the building's actual condition rather than arbitrary percentages of the operating budget.

existing_claim: The condo-capital-infra synthesis asserts an operative NS reserve-fund-study cadence of every 10 years, a site-inspection cadence of every 10 years, and a minimum 30-year planning horizon — placing NS at the longest base cycle in the Canadian provincial comparator set and framing the Atlantic provinces (alongside the North) as having 'more discretionary frameworks' relative to the prescriptive regimes in Ontario, BC, and Quebec. [[sources/docx-818ed0a0ce55]]
new_claim: Studies must be updated every five years, with site inspections, to confirm that funding levels are adequate to provide for future anticipated repairs/replacements; the physical analysis must include an inventory and assessment of each common element item that is expected to require major repair or replacement within at least 20 years of the date of the study — per the Condominium Act R.S., c. 85 last revised in 2022 by NS Bill No. 106 and Condominium Regulations under Section 33 and 46 of the Condominium Act, cited in the June 11, 2025 Sense Engineering Reserve Fund Study for Halifax Condominium Corporation No. 130.

existing_claim: The condo-capital-infra synthesis asserts ... a minimum 30-year planning horizon
new_claim: The Act requires a physical analysis covering items expected to require major repair or replacement within at least 20 years of the date of the study (statutory minimum); the financial analysis is at the preparer's discretion, with the Summer Gardens 2025 RFS using a 25-year forward projection — so the synthesis's 30-year minimum-planning-horizon framing is not supported as a statutory minimum.

existing_claim: Solume's deterministic-to-dashboard methodology framing (no probabilistic / Monte Carlo / Bayesian layer) per the January 23, 2025 Florida landing page positioning the product as converting 'outdated PDF reserve studies into interactive financial dashboards that adapt to Florida's unique maintenance needs' [[sources/web-2025-01-23-a1d]]
new_claim: Solume's November 15, 2025 press release reframes the methodology positioning as a 'living forecast' that 'updates reserve projections dynamically, using operating data, budgets, and vendor information to maintain current forecasts' — shifting the public framing from a static-PDF-to-interactive-dashboard axis to a static-periodic-paid-updates-vs-continuous-insight axis without disclosing any probabilistic methodology change [[sources/web-2025-11-15-556]]

existing_claim: Solume's January 2025 vendor-curated multi-state reserve-study state-requirements guide describes reserve-study practice in deterministic point-estimate terms throughout, with no engagement with probabilistic deterioration modeling, Monte Carlo aggregation, or distribution-based forecasting [[sources/web-2025-01-07-b6e]]
new_claim: Solume's November 2025 press release introduces a 'dynamic update' framing for reserve projections that, while still not invoking probabilistic methodology, materially differs from the static deterministic point-estimate framing surfaced in the January 2025 multi-state guide — reframing the vendor's methodology surface as 'continuous insight' from operating data, budgets, and vendor information rather than periodic deterministic recalculation [[sources/web-2025-11-15-556]]

existing_claim: Solume operationalizes multi-state coverage through jurisdiction-specific marketing landing pages: a January 23, 2025 FL-specific landing page at getsolume.com/florida-reserve-study confirms active FL SIRS / HB 913 GTM by the vendor — and a January 7, 2025 vendor-curated multi-state guide covers 13 US states.
new_claim: Solume's November 8, 2025 launch is framed as the platform's launch announcement: 'Solume has announced the launch of its AI-powered HOA and condo association management platform' / 'With its launch, Solume becomes one of the only HOA management platforms to incorporate dynamic reserve study management.'

existing_claim: Solume's product positioning frames it as converting 'outdated PDF reserve studies into interactive financial dashboards that adapt to Florida's unique maintenance needs' with a deterministic-to-dashboard methodology framing (no probabilistic / Monte Carlo / Bayesian layer).
new_claim: Solume's reserve study system 'updates in real time based on financial data, vendor expenses, and projected maintenance timelines' — framed as 'dynamic reserve study management' without methodology disclosure.

existing_claim: The synthesis frames NS specifically — and Atlantic Canada plus the North more generally — as operating under "more discretionary frameworks" relative to the prescriptive regimes in Ontario, BC, and Quebec.
new_claim: The Ontario regime documented in the CAO Best Practices Guide implements a tiered Class 1/2/3 cadence schema with Class 1 comprehensive within one year of declaration registration and alternating Class 2/Class 3 updates every three years — yielding higher per-corporation engagement density than NS's uniform 5-year cycle and operationally more prescriptive than the synthesis's framing of Ontario as the comparator-prescriptive regime would suggest at the cadence-architecture level (NS's 5-year uniform cycle delivers two same-scope studies per decade vs. ON's one comprehensive plus ~three updates per decade).

existing_claim: Studies typically itemize projects with anticipated costs greater than ~$5,000; the operating budget is assumed to fund minor repairs, routine maintenance activities, and replacements costing less than ~$5,000.
new_claim: Ontario codifies a $500 component-inventory threshold for items expected to require major repair or replacement within at least 30 years — a ten-fold lower cost cutoff than the NS operational ~$5,000 itemization convention, surfacing materially different definitions of what constitutes a reserve-fund-tracked component between the two provinces.

existing_claim: The six qualified-provider categories [effective July 1, 2025] are: (i) a person registered as a member in good standing with the Association of Professional Engineers and Geoscientists of British Columbia as a professional engineer or a professional licensee engineering; (ii) a person registered with the Architectural Institute of British Columbia as an architect or architectural technologist; (iii) a person registered with the Applied Science Technologists and Technicians of British Columbia as an applied science technologist or a certified technician; (iv) a person designated Accredited Appraiser Canadian Institute by the Appraisal Institute of Canada; (v) a certified reserve planner accredited by the Real Estate Institute of Canada; (vi) a person designated as Professional Quantity Surveyor by the Canadian Institute of Quantity Surveyors. [Source: web-2013-11-28-cda + web-2025-02-05-f51]
new_claim: BCFSA's January 26, 2026 blog post states that on October 27, 2025 the list of professionals who can provide a strata depreciation report was expanded to include licensed professional engineers, architectural technologists, and certified technicians — framing these three categories as added on October 27, 2025 rather than being part of the original July 1, 2025 qualified-provider list. Existing wiki claims (citing web-2013-11-28-cda and the Condo Control February 2025 summary) list these same three professions among the six categories effective July 1, 2025.

existing_claim: Cohen oversaw the October 2025 launch of Payables+, a significant upgrade to CINC's previous AP solution leveraging CINC's native Cephai+ AI technology to speed and simplify invoice ingestion, ledger coding, and digital payments
new_claim: On February 26, 2026, CINC announced the official launch of Payables+, characterized as 'the market's most advanced accounts payable (AP) automation solution' coupling Cephai+ AI with electronic payment capabilities powered by AvidXchange — framed as 'today announced the official launch of Payables+'

existing_claim: Spectrum Equity joined CINC Systems in 2019 and accelerated the company's growth.
new_claim: The June 10, 2020 CINC press release explicitly states that Spectrum is CINC's first institutional investor at the time of the June 10, 2020 announcement — placing Spectrum's public entry as CINC's first institutional investor in June 2020 rather than 2019.

existing_claim: On December 14, 2023, Spectrum continued as a co-investor in CINC alongside founder Bill Blanton, the management team, and incoming strategic investor Hg.
new_claim: In January of 2024, Hg Capital made a significant investment in CINC to accelerate the company's growth trajectory and institute rapid product development.

existing_claim: CEO of RISE Association Management Group as of September 16, 2025 [[sources/web-2025-09-16-709]].
new_claim: Managing Partner at RISE Management Group as of August 5, 2025 [[sources/web-2025-08-05-4b5]]. The August 2025 source explicitly identifies Jason Delgado as 'Managing Partner at RISE' rather than CEO — a five-week earlier title that differs from the September 2025 CEO framing.

existing_claim: The current §6.11(b)(i) CUDIC eligibility text dates from B.C. Reg. 68/2014, the amendment that substituted §6.11 of the Strata Property Regulation effective July 16, 2014.
new_claim: §6.11 of the Strata Property Regulation was further amended by Order in Council 101/2019, effective March 6, 2019, which substituted the prefatory language of §6.11(b) to require only that the deposit be eligible for CDIC or CUDIC insurance 'in whole or in part' — meaning the 'current' §6.11(b)(i) text post-dates the 2014 amendment.

existing_claim: AppFolio HOA Financials' published integration roster names five HOA-banking and check-processing partners — Alliance Association Bank, Pacific Premier Bank, First Citizens Bank, SmartStreet/Banc of California, and CheckAlt — with no mention of Western Alliance Bank.
new_claim: Western Alliance Bank's WA ConnectLive product page names AppFolio as one of 11 CAM software platforms its HOA API integrates with.

existing_claim: CheckAlt is the only non-bank entity in the AppFolio HOA partner roster, positioning it as a specialized lockbox/check-processing provider rather than a chartered depository.
new_claim: Western Alliance Bank — a chartered depository — exposes its own Lockbox, Positive Pay, and Integrated Payables treasury stack through WA ConnectLive with AppFolio as a named integration partner, indicating that AppFolio's roster of bank-and-check-processing partners is not exhaustive and that a chartered-bank alternative to CheckAlt is reachable from within the AppFolio ecosystem.

existing_claim: Paragraph 3 also establishes that interest earned on operating or reserve funds, plus rental and other incidental income, IS income of the corporation.
new_claim: Incidental income from the rental of common areas may be treated as income of the Corporation and generally will not affect the tax-exempt status of the Corporation; income that is not incidental will usually be considered to be income of the unit owners, if this is appropriate under the relevant provincial law.

existing_claim: A strata or condominium corporation must file Form T1044 with its T2 if the corporation's assets were more than $200,000 at the end of the fiscal year.
new_claim: T1044 filing trigger applies if assets > $200,000 during the fiscal year (or investment/property income > $10,000 or previous T1044 obligation).
